title: Lists
summary: A list stores values in order. You can use a list for books to read or scores in a game.
introduction: A list stores values in order. You can use a list for books to read or scores in a game. Make a small list. Find one item by its position, add an item and remove an item, checking the list after each change.
learningObjectives: Create lists and access items with indexes and slices
Add, remove and change items with append(), insert(), extend(), remove(), pop() and del
Sort and reverse lists with sort(), sorted() and a key function
Explain why assigning a list creates an alias and how to copy it properly

blocks.title: basics.py
blocks.code:
colours = ["red", "green", "blue"]
mixed = [1, "two", 3.0, [4, 5]]
empty = []

print(len(colours), colours[0], colours[-1])
print(mixed[3][1])
print(colours[1:3])
print(colours[::-1])
print("green" in colours, "pink" in colours)
print(empty, len(empty))

blocks.text: Square brackets create a list; items are separated by commas and may be of different types, although most lists hold one kind of thing. Indexing and slicing work exactly as for [strings](/tutorials/python/strings): `[0]` is the first item, `[-1]` the last, and a slice returns a new list. `mixed[3][1]` indexes into the inner list: item 3 is `[4, 5]`, and its item 1 is `5`.

Unlike strings, lists are **mutable**: you can assign to an index, append, insert and remove items, and the list object itself changes. Methods that change a list in place return `None`, not the list, which matters in a moment.

blocks.title: modify.py
blocks.code:
tasks = ["write", "test"]
tasks.append("deploy")                # add at the end
tasks.insert(0, "plan")               # add at a position
tasks.extend(["celebrate", "rest"])   # add several at once
print(tasks)

tasks[1] = "design"                   # replace by index
print(tasks)

tasks.remove("rest")                  # remove by value (first match)
last = tasks.pop()                    # remove and return the last item
first = tasks.pop(0)                  # or the item at an index
del tasks[0]                          # remove by index without returning
print(tasks, last, first)
print(tasks.index("test"), tasks.count("test"))

rows: Add one item at the end
Add `x` at index `i`, shifting the rest right
Add every item of another list, tuple or range
Remove the first item equal to `x`; `ValueError` if absent
Remove and return the item at `i` (the last by default)
Find the first position of `x`, count its occurrences

blocks.title: sorting.py
blocks.code:
numbers = [42, 7, 19, 3]
numbers.sort()
print(numbers)
numbers.sort(reverse=True)
print(numbers)

names = ["mina", "Ravi", "sofia"]
print(sorted(names))
print(sorted(names, key=str.lower))
print(names)

words = ["kiwi", "fig", "banana"]
print(sorted(words, key=len))
print(max(numbers), min(words))

blocks.text: `sort()` rearranges the list in place; `sorted()` leaves the original alone and returns a new sorted list, and it works on any iterable. Both accept `reverse=True` and a `key` function that says what to compare: `str.lower` for case-insensitive order, `len` for length. Capital letters sort before lower-case ones because of their Unicode codes, which is why `"Ravi"` came first in the plain sort. `min()` and `max()` use the same ordering.

blocks.title: sort() returns None
blocks.text: `numbers = numbers.sort()` is a classic bug: `sort()` changes the list in place and returns `None`, so the variable now holds `None` and the next line fails with `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`. Either call `numbers.sort()` on its own line or write `numbers = sorted(numbers)`. The same applies to `append()`, `reverse()` and every other in-place method.

blocks.title: copies.py
blocks.code:
original = [1, 2, 3]
alias = original          # a second name for the same list
alias.append(4)
print(original, alias)
print(original is alias)

duplicate = original.copy()   # or original[:] or list(original)
duplicate.append(5)
print(original, duplicate)
print(original is duplicate, original == duplicate)

blocks.text: Assignment never copies. `alias = original` makes two names for one list, so a change made through either name shows up in both, and `is` confirms they are the same object. `copy()`, a full slice `[:]` or `list(original)` creates a new list with the same items, after which the two lead separate lives. The same rule applies to lists passed into functions: the function receives the list itself, not a copy, so anything it appends is visible to the caller.
The most common list pattern is to start empty and append inside a loop. Nested lists (a list of lists) represent grids and tables; index the row first, then the column.

blocks.title: build.py
blocks.code:
prices = [19.99, 5.49, 3.0]
with_tax = []
for price in prices:
    with_tax.append(round(price * 1.2, 2))
print(with_tax)
print(round(sum(with_tax), 2), max(prices))

for position, price in enumerate(prices):
    print(position, price)

matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
print(matrix[1][2], len(matrix), len(matrix[0]))

blocks.title: Shorter with a comprehension
blocks.text: The append-in-a-loop pattern is so common that Python has a one-line form for it: `[round(p * 1.2, 2) for p in prices]`. The [Comprehensions](/tutorials/python/comprehensions) lesson covers it once you are comfortable with loops and lists.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: `b = a` does not copy; both names refer to the same list, so appending through `b` makes the list four items long for `a` as well.

questions.question: Which call removes the last item of `items` and gives it back to you?
questions.explanation: `pop()` removes and returns the last item. `del items[-1]` removes it without returning it, `remove()` takes a value rather than a position, and there is no `delete()` method.

seo.title: Python Lists – Indexing, Methods, Sorting and Copying
seo.description: Learn Python lists: create and index them, append, insert and remove items, sort with sort() and sorted(), and understand aliasing versus copying.
